title: The Oceans · Episode 2
chapters: Living light: the glow of bioluminescence

units.t: The Oceans. Episode two.
In this episode: Into the Challenger Deep, Living light: the glow of bioluminescence and Sharks: fear versus facts.
Part one. Into the Challenger Deep.
The deepest point in the ocean lies nearly 11 kilometres down, under pressure that could crush a submarine.
Two men first reached it in 1960 in a craft held up by petrol.
The deepest place.
In the western Pacific lies the Mariana Trench, a scar on the seafloor over 2,500 kilometres long, formed where one tectonic plate dives beneath another.
At its southern end is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known place in the oceans, about 10,900 metres down by most recent measurements.
Put Mount Everest at the bottom and its summit would still sit more than two kilometres underwater.
It is named after HMS Challenger, whose 1870s scientific voyage took a sounding there.
Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly one atmosphere of pressure, so at the bottom it is more than a thousand times that at sea level, over a tonne on every square centimetre.
An ordinary submarine would be crushed.
The bathyscaphe.
A crewed vessel needs a thick sphere, which spreads pressure evenly, but such a sphere sinks like a stone.
The question was how to float back up.
The solution came from the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard, who had flown balloons into the stratosphere.
His bathyscaphe, meaning "deep boat", was essentially an underwater balloon: a large petrol-filled float above a small, thick steel crew sphere.
Petrol is lighter than water and compresses very little, so it keeps providing lift under enormous pressure.
To descend, the craft carried tonnes of iron pellets as ballast, held by electromagnets.
To rise, the crew released the pellets.
Auguste and his son Jacques built the Trieste in Italy in the 1950s, and the US Navy later bought it.
23 January 1960.
On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh squeezed into the Trieste's cramped sphere, only about two metres across inside.
The descent took nearly five hours.
Partway down they heard a loud crack, and later found that an outer window had fractured, though the inner structure held.
They settled onto the seabed, nearly 11 kilometres down, and spent only around twenty minutes there.
Their landing stirred up fine sediment that made photographs impossible.
Piccard reported seeing a flatfish through the porthole, but many biologists now doubt this, since fish are not thought to survive at that depth.
The ascent took over three hours, and both men returned to a hero's welcome.
Fifty-two years later.
After the Trieste, no human went back for fifty-two years.
Uncrewed vehicles such as Japan's Kaiko reached the deep in the 1990s, while crewed submersibles like Alvin explored shallower sites.
Attention flowed to the Space Race, and it was said that more people had walked on the Moon than visited the deepest ocean.
On 26 March 2012 filmmaker James Cameron dived alone in Deepsea Challenger, a vertical, torpedo-like submersible designed and built mostly in Sydney, with Australian engineer Ron Allum.
It used syntactic foam, packed with tiny hollow glass spheres, for buoyancy instead of a petrol float.
The descent took about two and a half hours, and he spent around three hours at the bottom before a hydraulic fault cut his time short.
He described a lunar-like, desolate landscape.
The deep becomes reachable.
In 2019 the American explorer Victor Vescovo began repeated dives in the Limiting Factor, a titanium-hulled submersible designed to reach the bottom of any ocean again and again.
On his Five Deeps Expedition he reached the deepest points of all five oceans.
Over the following years the craft took a number of people to the Challenger Deep.
In June 2020, Kathryn Sullivan, a former NASA astronaut and the first American woman to walk in space, became the first woman to reach it.
Dives have also brought sobering news, as researchers have reported plastic debris and human-made pollutants even in the deepest trenches.
The bottom of the world is no longer out of reach, and neither, it turns out, is our rubbish.
The key idea: The Challenger Deep is nearly 11 kilometres down, where pressure is over a thousand times that at the surface.
Part two. Living light: the glow of bioluminescence.
In the darkest places on Earth, animals make their own light.
They use it to hunt, hide, flirt and even call the police on their attackers.
Light from chemistry.
Bioluminescence is cold light made by life.
Usually a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase, and the energy comes out as light rather than heat.
Different groups evolved their own versions, so glowing has arisen independently dozens of times.
Some animals make the light themselves.
Many deep-sea fish instead house glowing bacteria in special organs.
The sea is where it thrives.
Off California, researchers found roughly three-quarters of the deep-water animals they observed could make light.
Most is blue or blue-green, which travels furthest in sea water.
Reds fade within metres.
Some dragonfish make red light near their eyes and can see it, a private searchlight for prey that cannot.
Hiding in plain light.
In the ocean's twilight zone, faint light filters down from above.
Any animal swimming there casts a dark silhouette that predators below can spot.
Many fish, squid and shrimps solve this by lighting up their undersides to match the glow overhead, so their outline disappears.
This is called counter-illumination.
Hatchetfish use rows of light organs along their bellies.
The Hawaiian bobtail squid uses glowing bacteria called Vibrio fischeri, held in a light organ.
Each morning it expels most of them and regrows the colony, and it can adjust its brightness to match moonlight.
It is invisibility achieved by adding light rather than taking it away.
Lures, alarms, smoke screens.
The deep-sea anglerfish dangles a bacteria-lit lure from a modified fin spine on its head and swallows whatever comes to investigate.
Light also serves defence.
Tiny plankton flash when disturbed, and biologists have proposed a burglar alarm effect: the flash may attract larger predators that attack whatever is attacking the plankton.
Certain jellyfish give off pinwheels of light when grabbed, perhaps for the same reason.
Others use light as a smoke screen.
Some deep-sea shrimps and squid squirt glowing fluid instead of dark ink, and the vampire squid can release sticky, glowing mucus.
A predator lunging at the bright cloud may miss the animal slipping away into the dark.
Fireflies and glow-worms.
Fireflies are actually beetles, and their flashes are a courtship language.
Males flash species-specific patterns in flight, and females answer from the ground with timed signals.
Some females exploit this.
In North America, females of the genus Photuris mimic the replies of another genus, lure in eager males and eat them.
Australia and New Zealand have a different light show.
The glow-worms of caves and damp gullies, such as Springbrook in Queensland or Waitomo in New Zealand, are not worms but the larvae of fungus gnats.
They hang sticky silk threads from the ceiling and glow blue to attract small flying insects, which become trapped and are reeled in.
Glowing seas, borrowed light.
Sometimes the glow comes to the shore.
Tiny single-celled plankton called dinoflagellates flash when disturbed, so breaking waves, paddling feet and kayak strokes can light up electric blue.
Beaches in Tasmania, Jervis Bay and many places overseas occasionally put on this display.
Some fungi glow too, including Australia's ghost fungus, which shines a faint green on rotting wood at night.
Scientists have borrowed nature's lights.

Firefly luciferase is used in laboratories to detect chemical activity, and a green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish became a revolutionary tool for tagging cells and genes, earning the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
A glow first noticed in the sea now helps researchers watch diseases develop.
The key idea: Bioluminescence is cold light made by a chemical reaction in a living thing, and most of it happens in the sea.
Part three. Sharks: fear versus facts.
Sharks are older than trees, come in more than 500 species and are far more at risk from us than we are from them.
Older than trees.
Sharks appeared more than 400 million years ago, earlier than trees, which evolved roughly 385 million years ago, and long before dinosaurs.
They have survived several mass extinctions.
Their skeletons are made of cartilage, the flexible material in your nose and ears, which is why fossil sharks are mostly known from teeth.
Sharks replace their teeth throughout life, sometimes thousands over a lifetime.
The extinct megalodon, which died out around 3.
6 million years ago, may have reached 15 metres or more.
There are over 500 known species, and most look nothing like the movie villain.
The dwarf lanternshark is about 20 centimetres long and glows in the deep sea.
Wobbegongs lie camouflaged on Australian reefs like shaggy rugs.
Giants and survivors.
The whale shark, the largest fish in the world, can exceed 12 metres yet feeds on plankton.
Each year it gathers at Ningaloo Reef in WA.
The Greenland shark grows so slowly that a 2016 study estimated some live for several centuries, possibly around 400 years, making it the longest-lived known vertebrate.
Sharks also reproduce differently from most fish, which scatter huge numbers of tiny eggs.
Sharks produce a few large, well-developed young, and fertilisation happens inside the female.
Some species lay eggs in tough cases; the Port Jackson shark wedges its corkscrew-shaped egg cases into rocky crevices.
Many give birth to live pups, and hammerheads and bull sharks nourish their young through a placenta-like connection.
Cannibal siblings.
The grey nurse shark goes further than most.
In each of the mother's two uteri, the first embryo to develop eats its smaller siblings and spare eggs.
A litter is usually just two pups, born every second year, and the pups get no parental care once born.
They must fend for themselves from day one.
This slow, low-numbers way of reproducing is why many sharks struggle to recover when their numbers fall.
Sharks that produce only a few young, mature late and grow slowly cannot quickly replace the animals that are lost.
The real risk.
Shark bites are frightening and heavily reported, but rare.
Worldwide, researchers typically record around 50 to 80 confirmed unprovoked bites a year, with fatalities usually in single figures.
In Australia, a few people die from shark bites in a typical year, while roughly a hundred or more drown along the coast.
Only a handful of species cause most serious bites, chiefly the white, tiger and bull shark.
The danger runs the other way.
A widely cited 2013 study estimated that humans kill around 100 million sharks a year, through fishing, bycatch and the fin trade.
A major 2021 study found oceanic sharks and rays had fallen by about 70% since 1970, and around a third of shark and ray species are now threatened.
The east coast grey nurse shark is listed as critically endangered.
Why sharks matter.
As predators and scavengers, sharks shape whole ecosystems.
When large sharks disappear, effects ripple down the food chain, sometimes letting prey overgraze seagrass or reefs.
Tiger sharks are thought to help protect seagrass in Shark Bay, WA, by keeping grazing turtles and dugongs on the move.
Australia uses nets, baited drumlines, drones, tagging and alert apps, and which mix works best is debated, partly because nets also catch turtles, dolphins and harmless sharks.
You can lower your own risk: swim at patrolled beaches between the flags, avoid dawn, dusk and murky water, and stay clear of baitfish, birds and people fishing.
Rips are the far bigger danger.
The key idea: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years, longer than trees, and come in more than 500 species, from hand-sized to bus-sized.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why can't an ordinary submarine reach the Challenger Deep?
Answer. Pressure over a thousand times sea level would crush it.
Question two. What usually produces the light in bioluminescence?
Answer. Luciferin reacting with oxygen and an enzyme.
Question three. Which of these appeared on Earth first?
Answer. Sharks.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
